title: Gelato: Graph Edit Distance via Autoregressive Matching
one_liner: A neural network learns to match nodes between two graphs one pair at a time, capturing which earlier choices affect which later ones, to solve a famously hard graph comparison problem much faster than traditional solvers.
lead: When you want to know how different two graphs are (e.g., comparing molecular structures or road networks), you need to find the cheapest sequence of edits to turn one into the other. This is called the graph edit distance problem, and it is computationally exhausting — traditional solvers give up on graphs with more than 20 nodes. Gelato uses a neural network to learn patterns in how to match nodes across graphs, predicting the best pair to link at each step.

paras: Comparing two graphs means finding how different they are. If you have a graph with nodes (like cities) and edges (like roads between them), and you want to check if it is the same as another graph, you need to find a one-to-one pairing of nodes that preserves as many edges as possible. The cost of the pairing is how many edits you need to make: adding edges, removing edges, or changing node labels.

The hard part: if you have 20 nodes in each graph, there are twenty-factorial possible pairings (twenty times nineteen times eighteen and so on, which is an astronomically large number). Traditional solvers use clever tricks to prune this search space, but they still exhaust their memory and time on graphs bigger than 20 nodes. Simpler heuristics (greedy algorithms that just pick the best-looking pair at each step without thinking ahead) run fast but often miss the truly cheapest pairing.
The naive approach: try all pairings, or use a greedy heuristic. Both fail — exhaustive search is impossible, and greedy misses the global optimum.

callout.html: The paper teaches a neural network to predict which two nodes should be matched next, one pair at a time, using what it learned from earlier matches.

panels.title: 2. A naive greedy choice
panels.caption: A greedy method picks node pairs one at a time based only on local similarity, often backing into a dead end.

panels.title: 3. Gelato looks ahead
panels.caption: Gelato remembers earlier matches and adjusts, choosing pairs that leave good options for the next step.

panels.title: 4. Step-by-step matching

panels.title: 5. Final pairing with low cost
panels.caption: The result is a matching with fewer edits needed than a greedy or random pairing would need.

steps.text: A graph neural network (a model that learns from the connectivity pattern) reads both graphs and builds a representation for each node that captures its role.
The network scores how well each node in graph A matches each node in graph B, and picks the best pair.

steps.b: Condition the next prediction on what is done
steps.text: Once that pair is locked in, the network re-computes scores for remaining nodes, taking into account that some matches are already settled.

steps.b: Repeat until all (or enough) nodes are matched
steps.text: Step by step, the network picks the next-best pair, aware of the full history of earlier choices.

steps.b: Compute the edit cost of the matching
steps.text: Count how many edge additions and deletions are needed to make one graph match the other given the pairing.

object.h2: The one thing the paper changes
paras: Instead of a greedy or exhaustive search, Gelato uses a neural network to pick which nodes to match. The object is: the sequence of node pairs (the matching itself).

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: structural dependency depth
hidden.name: How much earlier matches constrain later ones
paras: When you match node A1 to B3, that choice affects which nodes are left and how similar they are to the remaining graph B nodes. Some matches unlock good next choices; others paint you into a corner. The paper does not name this explicitly, but the core hidden quantity is: the degree to which each match depends on the structure captured in earlier matches.

Gelato measures this through the neural network's attention mechanism (the learned weights that decide how much each node pays attention to each edge and neighbor node). By conditioning each new prediction on the full history of locked matches, the network implicitly tracks which structural patterns matter most for the remaining choices. The network learns to avoid dead-end pairings by recognizing when a match leaves good structural room for future steps.

heat.caption: Darker means more impact on avoiding dead-end matchings.

reads.html: When you lock in one match, you shrink the problem. Gelato learns which matches leave you with good next options (lots of high-similarity pairs left) versus bad ones (few good pairs left). That learned pattern is the hidden quantity.

The paper uses a graph neural network encoder to build node embeddings (learned descriptions of each node based on its neighbors and features), then decodes one match at a time. At each step, it scores remaining nodes given the matched pairs so far. By basing each score on the pairs already locked in, the network captures which decisions constrain which future options.

mechanism.h2: Why predicting one pair at a time works
paras: The reason Gelato succeeds is that matching is a sequential decision problem, and breaking it into steps lets the network learn which early choices lead to good late choices. A graph neural network can learn from training examples (you show it many graph pairs with good matchings), whereas a fixed search algorithm cannot adapt. When the network has already matched two pairs and is deciding the third, it has learned from training: 'when the remaining nodes look like this pattern, pairing these two nodes together leaves me with better options for the next step.' It learned this because training data showed that such choices led to lower total edit costs.

Making one prediction at a time (one pair per step) matters because each prediction can incorporate the history. A model that predicted all matches at once would have to predict them independently of each other, ignoring which pairs were already locked. By recomputing match scores based only on unmatched nodes after each step, the model avoids impossible pairings and makes choices that leave good options for the next step. Training teaches the network: greedy choices that look good right now often trap you into bad later choices; instead, learn which early matches leave you with good next options.

stages.s: Two graphs: nodes, edges, node features (e.g., atom types)
Graph neural network encodes each node as a learned vector (capturing neighborhood and role)
Score each unmatched pair by dot-product (vector multiplication); pick the highest score
Lock that pair; recompute representations using only unmatched nodes
A complete node-pair matching; compute edit cost from edge differences

math.words: At each step, score each unmatched node-pair by the dot product (multiply and sum) of their learned vectors, then pick the pair with the highest score. After locking a pair, update the learned vectors to reflect that some nodes are now unavailable.
math.equation: score(i, j) = encode(node_i) · encode(node_j) for all unmatched (i, j); pick argmax(score); lock pair; update encode() to zero out matched nodes.
symbols: how well node i in graph A matches node j in graph B
the learned vector for node i, built by the graph neural network
dot product: multiply element-wise and sum to get one number
pick the pair with the highest score
mark that pair as chosen and remove both nodes from future scoring

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Graph A has nodes 1, 2, 3; Graph B has nodes X, Y, Z.
Best for A1 is B_X (0.62). Check A2·B_Y = 0.3*0.2 + 0.9*0.8 = 0.06 + 0.72 = 0.78. Best pair overall: A1→B_X. Lock it.
Step 2: only A2, A3, B_Y, B_Z remain. A2·B_Y = 0.78 (best). Lock A2→B_Y. A3→B_Z is forced.
Matching: A1→B_X, A2→B_Y, A3→B_Z. Now count edge edits: if A1-A2 is an edge but B_X-B_Y is not, that costs 1 deletion, etc.

math.note: The network learns these dot-product vectors from training data, so high scores correlate with low-cost matchings in that data.

charts.title: Traditional solvers
charts.note: Exact solvers work well up to 20 nodes, then collapse. Heuristics run anywhere but produce poor matchings.

charts.title: Gelato
charts.note: Neural networks generalize to larger graphs if trained on a variety of sizes. Gelato remains fast and accurate even on unseen sizes.

items.b: Training data does not cover the types you test on.
items.html: If training examples are small graphs from one domain (e.g., social networks), and you test on large chemical structures, the learned patterns may not work. The network has never seen the structural patterns of the new domain, so it cannot recognize which matches are good. However, the paper shows Gelato generalizes better than rule-based baselines because neural networks can extract structure from features even when domain is new, and training on graphs of many sizes helps it handle unseen sizes.

items.b: A greedy early choice really does close off the best matching.
items.html: Even if the network tries to look ahead, if it makes a locally good but globally bad first match, it cannot backtrack. Once locked, a pair stays locked. This is rare if training data shows clearly that such mistakes lead to high costs, but it can happen on unusual graph structures the network did not see in training.

If nodes have unclear features (e.g., all nodes are generic blobs with the same label), the network has little to go on. Without strong node signals, the network must rely only on edge patterns, which is harder. The paper tests this and finds the network works better with clearer labels because it has more signal to distinguish which nodes should pair together.

Train on a diverse set of graphs with ground-truth matchings (or loss-based feedback). The network learns to recognize structural patterns that correlate with cheap matchings. At test time, even on unseen graph sizes, it applies those learned patterns because the structure of graph matching is consistent across sizes.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple graph-matching demo that lets you generate two random graphs (10–15 nodes each), run Gelato's matching, and show the edit cost. Then run a greedy heuristic on the same pair. You will see that Gelato's cost is lower because the network learned from training data which early matches leave better options later, while the greedy heuristic picks the best-looking pair right now without thinking ahead. For extra credit, train a tiny Gelato network on a small synthetic dataset of graph pairs with ground-truth costs, then test it on a held-out pair and compare to a solver (or greedy baseline).
demo.metric_eq: edit_cost = (edges in A but not matched to edges in B) + (edges in B but not matched to edges in A)
demo.closing: The demo must show that predicting pairs one at a time (aware of history) avoids the greedy trap where a locally good choice locks you into globally bad options.
